content: The 2019 Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services (HTS), published by the World Health Organization (WHO), provide comprehensive and evidence-based recommendations for HIV testing across various settings and populations. These guidelines aim to support Member States, program managers, healthcare workers, and other stakeholders in achieving national and international goals to end the HIV epidemic as a public health threat by 2030. The guidelines were first introduced in 2015 to assist in meeting the United Nations' 90-90-90 global HIV targets, particularly the goal of diagnosing 90% of all individuals living with HIV. In 2016, WHO released a supplement addressing new approaches, such as HIV self-testing (HIVST) and provider-assisted referral. Since then, additional evidence and emerging issues have necessitated updates to the guidance. The 2019 update includes revised recommendations on HIVST and introduces new recommendations on social network-based HIV testing approaches and the discontinuation of western blotting in national testing strategies. The guidelines also provide operational guidance on demand creation, messaging, and implementation considerations for priority populations. They emphasize optimizing the use of dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests, strategic planning, and resource rationalization, such as identifying optimal time points for maternal retesting during pregnancy and postpartum. Key objectives of the guidelines include: Offering evidence-based recommendations for HTS. Supporting the scale-up of strategic, evidence-based HTS approaches in both facility and community settings to reach undiagnosed individuals. Ensuring effective linkage to prevention, treatment, and care services for those tested. Promoting the integration of HIV testing with other relevant health services. Rationalizing the use of retesting during late pregnancy and postpartum, and prioritizing dual HIV/syphilis rapid tests in antenatal care. Encouraging the implementation of quality HTS using recommended testing strategies while discontinuing western blotting. Providing guidance for strategic planning and resource optimization to achieve global and national HIV goals. Advocating for greater national and global commitment to effective and efficient HTS as a critical component of the HIV response. The guidelines address HTS for key populations, the general population, pregnant and postpartum women, couples and partners, adolescents, young people, migrants, refugees, displaced individuals, and other vulnerable groups. The development of these guidelines involved a rigorous process led by the WHO HIV Department, with input from a Guideline Steering Group (SG), an independent Guideline Development Group (GDG), and an external peer review group. The GDG, comprising experts from diverse regions and disciplines, reviewed evidence, conducted systematic reviews, and provided recommendations on western blotting, social network-based HTS approaches, and HIVST. They also developed a good practice statement on evidence-based approaches and the use of incentives for demand creation.
